newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Study finds up to 10 pct of Swiss are poor.
newsitem.headline: Study finds up to 10 pct of Swiss are poor.

text.p: As many as one in 10 people is poor in Switzerland, which is one of the richest countries in the world, according to the first national survey of poverty.

The study said that although Switzerland has no official poverty line the closest thing is the limit for drawing welfare benefits -- a maximum monthly income of 2,100 Swiss francs ($1,481) for a single-person household.

The Swiss National Science Foundation study of more than 6,000 Swiss nationals and foreign residents found 9.8 percent, representing nationally about 680,000 people, fell below income guidelines for welfare.
Under another standard, 1,800 Swiss francs per month as set by the Swiss Conference for Public Assistance, 5.6 percent or 390,000 people lived in poverty.
The World Bank ranked Switzerland as the second-richest nation in 1994 with Gross National Product -- the value of all goods and services -- at $37,180 per capita.

Poverty was most common among foreign residents -- who make up 19 percent of a population nearing seven million -- as well as the self-employed, men who live alone, divorced women and single mothers, the study said.
"The survey showed that the poverty rate is clearly higher among foreign residents than Swiss nationals -- every fourth poor person is a foreign citizen," it said.
Switzerland is ranked among the world's richest countries, powered by globally active banks, a large export industry and stable currency.
The science foundation said the survey was based on 1992 data, so it did include most effects of economic stagnation that has kept Swiss growth at around zero since 1991.

It also said the gap between rich and poor had widened between 1982 and 1992 as the wealthiest 10 percent of the population took an ever larger share of national income and assets, but provided no detailed figures.
